## Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

- Explain why good documentation is worth developing
- Describe the different ways in which code can be documented
- Understand the major features of good documentation

## Prerequisites

There are no technical prerequisites of this module, although you can refer to [our module on package building](link) to learn more about how documentation is structured in R packages.

## Motivation

The purpose of code documentation is to provide additional, human-readable information alongside our code. This can include:

- What the code aims to achieve, in the wider context of the project. For example, why was 30 degrees north chosen as a cut-off for the latitude of our occurrences?
- Why the code was written as it was. For example, a for loop was used instead of a more efficient vectorised function, because human readability is a priority in our project and this is more easily understandable.
- Additional thought process. For example, annotation can be used to flag problematic parts of the code during the development process.
- Intended usage. For example, details can be given about what the intended inputs and outputs of a novel function were at the time of writing.
- Limitations of the code. For example, noting that the current implementation cannot handle inputs that include NA values.

As we note that code documentation has multiple purposes, this also means that it has many potential readers, including:

- Your future self. Documenting code well helps you to understand old code faster, and can remind you of the previous learning process, helping to prevent repeated mistakes.
- Your collaborators. Well documented code is much easier to review (see [our module on code review](link)). It also helps others to maintain and update code which you wrote but no longer work on.
- Your users. Depending on the type of code, this can mean many different things - a point we will return to later.

It's also worth remembering that many of us strive to make our work FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable and reproducible). Our code is only reproducible, or even better, reusable, if potential users can understand exactly what it does and why: documentation is essential to this process.

Good documentation takes time, and in our 'publish or perish' culture, many researchers consider that this may not be time well spent. However, it's worth remembering that time spent documenting code as you write it can save you from getting confused and repeating errors later. It helps you to conduct collaborative coding more effectively, meaning it's easier to outsource tasks to others. Robust and reusable code is also more likely to allow others to use your tool and build on your work, and therefore bring in citations.

The purpose of this guide is to give you an overview of code documentation, alongside tips and tricks for writing good documentation, to help you document your code in an effective but time-efficient manner.

## What is documentation?

- Code annotation
- Vignettes
- Formal help files
- READMEs
- Contribution guides? Higher level

## Topics to include

Talk about the philosophy, who is your audience and how can you give them what they need to know?

Do clear object names remove the need for annotation?

Use of simpler English to make it more understandable, helps with translation also 

People using AI as a shortcut to generating documentation, what does this risk? Better for ‘what’ than ‘why’, this is more or less relevant for different elements of the documentation

How to select examples, vignette topics

Code annotation
